questions.title: Minimum Window Substring — smallest substring in A containing all chars of B
questions.body: Given strings A and B, find the smallest substring in A which contains all characters in B. This is the classic Minimum Window Substring problem. MMT specifically asked candidates to code it in Java and explicitly noted Java hard requirement after this question.
questions.answer:
Problem: Find the smallest substring of A that contains every character of B (with multiplicity).

Idea — sliding window + two frequency maps:

  1. Build need: counts of chars required from B. Track missing = how many chars still needed.
  2. Expand right. When you cover a needed char, decrement missing.
  3. While the window is valid (missing == 0), shrink left to minimise length and record the best [L,R].
  4. When shrinking removes a needed char, increment missing again.

Why it works: every time the window becomes valid you have a candidate; shrinking finds the leftmost start for that right endpoint. Over all right endpoints you cover the global minimum.

Complexity: O(|A| + |B|) time, O(charset) space. Edge cases: empty B; B longer than A; duplicate chars in B; no valid window → return empty.

Interview tip: dry-run on A="ADOBECODEBANC", B="ABC". Mention Java is often required at MMT even if you sketch C++.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SDE-2 GFG 2021, MMT Campus, Code360 2022
questions.hint: Sliding window with two frequency maps. Expand right, shrink left when valid. Track best window.

questions.title: Subarray with Sum Zero — find any subarray whose sum = 0
questions.body: Given an array, find any subarray which has a sum of 0. Asked in the SDE/SSE-2 DSA round (LeetCode Discuss, Oct 2024).
questions.answer:
Problem: Detect any contiguous subarray whose sum is 0 (or return its indices).

Idea — prefix sums + HashMap: let pref[i] = a[0]+…+a[i]. If pref[j] == pref[i-1], then a[i..j] sums to 0. Also if pref[j] == 0, a[0..j] works.

  1. Scan left→right maintaining running sum s.
  2. Store first index where each prefix appeared (or a set if you only need yes/no).
  3. On seeing a repeated prefix (or 0), you found a zero-sum subarray.

Complexity: O(N) time, O(N) space. Edge cases: single 0; negatives; multiple answers — any is fine unless asked for longest/shortest.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Approach: Prefix sum + HashMap. If same prefix sum appears twice, the subarray between them sums to 0.

questions.title: Merge K Sorted Arrays / Linked Lists
questions.body: Merge 2 sorted arrays and Merge K sorted linked lists appeared together in a single SDE-2 Round 1. Union of two sorted arrays (SDE-1 Aug 2024) is a variant. All test in-place merge, heap-based K-way merge.
questions.answer:
Problem: Merge K sorted linked lists into one sorted list.

Idea — min-heap of size K:

  1. Push the head of each non-empty list into a min-heap keyed by node value.
  2. Repeatedly pop the smallest node, append to the result, and push that node’s next if any.

Why heap: you always need the global minimum among K frontiers — heap gives O(log K) per extract.

Complexity: O(N log K) time for N total nodes, O(K) heap space. Pitfalls: null lists in the input array; define a proper ListNode constructor (dummy head pattern).

Alternatives: pairwise merge (like merge-sort) also O(N log K); divide-and-conquer merging of lists.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SDE-2 GFG 2021, SDE-1 Naukri Aug 2024
questions.hint: Min-heap of size K — always extract minimum, push next from same list.

questions.title: Jump Game II — minimum number of jumps (+ return jump indexes)
questions.answer:
Problem: Minimum jumps to reach the last index (Jump Game II). Optionally reconstruct jump positions.

Idea — greedy BFS layers: treat indices reachable with the same jump count as a “layer”.

  1. Maintain curEnd (end of current jump’s reach) and farthest (furthest you can reach while scanning the layer).
  2. When i == curEnd, you must take another jump: jumps++, set curEnd = farthest.

Path variant: while scanning each layer, record the first parent that reaches each new index; reconstruct from n-1 back to 0. Cap reach at n-1 to avoid out-of-bounds.

Complexity: O(N) time / O(1) space for count; O(N) space for path. Edge: already at end (n≤1); unreachable array (path returns empty).

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SSE-2 LeetCode Discuss Nov 2023, CodingKaro
questions.hint: Greedy: track current range end and furthest reachable. When pointer hits current end, increment jump count.

questions.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
questions.body: Explicitly listed as the first question in SDE-2 Round 1 (GFG 2021). Sort + merge sweep pattern.
questions.answer:
Problem: Merge all overlapping intervals.

Idea:

  1. Sort by start time.
  2. Scan: if current start ≤ last merged end, extend end = max(end, current.end); else push a new interval.

Why sort: after sorting, overlaps can only involve the previous interval in the result — one linear pass.

Complexity: O(N log N) sort + O(N). Edge: touching intervals [1,2][2,3] — decide if inclusive merge (usually yes); empty input; single interval.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Sort intervals by start. Scan and merge when current.start <= last.end; else push new interval.

questions.title: Multiply Two Large Integers as Strings
questions.body: SDE-2 Round 1 (LeetCode Discuss 2025). Candidate was allowed Python. Long multiplication simulation.
questions.answer:
Problem: Multiply two non-negative integers given as strings (may not fit in 64-bit).

Idea — grade-school multiplication:

  1. Result array of size n+m. For digits num1[i], num2[j], add product into pos[i+j+1], carry into pos[i+j].
  2. Walk the array converting digits to a string; skip leading zeros.

Complexity: O(n·m) time, O(n+m) space. Edge: either operand "0"; leading zeros in input (normalise).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Find All Pairs with Given Sum in Two Arrays
questions.body: Given two arrays, print all pairs that sum to K. Technical Round 1 (Software Engineer, 2020). Hashmap approach to O(N).
questions.answer:
Problem: All pairs (a from A, b from B) with a+b = K.

Idea: Put all of A into a multiset/map (or set if uniqueness allowed). For each b in B, check if K-b exists in A.

If duplicates matter: use frequency maps, not a plain set — a set drops duplicate keys and under-counts pairs.

Complexity: O(N+M) expected with hashing. Follow-up: sorted arrays → two pointers without extra space.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
questions.body: Appeared in SSE-2 Round 2 alongside Jump Game II (Nov 2023, IIT candidate).
questions.answer:
Problem: Exists indices i < j < k with a[i] < a[j] < a[k]?

Idea — one pass, track two minima:

  1. first = smallest so far; second = smallest number that already has a smaller to its left.
  2. On seeing x: if x <= first update first; else if x <= second update second; else you found a third → true.

Complexity: O(N) time, O(1) space. Beat the O(N²) DP. Trap: equalities — use strict < as stated.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Maximum j–i such that arr[j] > arr[i]
questions.body: Technical Round 2 (Software Engineer 2020). O(n) time, O(n) space approach using prefix min array and suffix max array.
questions.answer:
Problem: Maximise j−i subject to arr[j] > arr[i] (or ≥ depending on statement — confirm with interviewer).

Idea — left-min / right-max + two pointers:

  1. Lmin[i] = min on [0..i]; Rmax[j] = max on [j..n-1].
  2. Two pointers from left/right: if Lmin[i] < Rmax[j] (or ≤), update answer and try larger span by moving j; else move i.

Complexity: O(N). Clarify strict vs non-strict comparison — GFG “Maximum Index” often uses ≤.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Pre-compute leftMin[] and rightMax[], then use two-pointer to find max (j-i).

questions.title: Maximize Sum Picking K Elements from Either Side
questions.body: SSE BLR 2022 (Offer received). Pick exactly K elements from left or right ends, maximize sum. Sliding window of size (n-k) on the complement.
questions.answer:
Problem: Pick exactly K elements from either end of the array; maximise their sum.

Equivalence: leaving a contiguous middle of length n−K. Minimising that middle sum maximises the ends’ sum.

  1. Compute total sum; find minimum sum subarray of length n−K (sliding window); answer = total − that min.
  2. Or explicitly try taking i from left and K−i from right using prefix/suffix sums.

Complexity: O(N). Edge: K=n (take all); K=0.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Equivalent to minimising the sum of a middle window of length n−K (complement of picks from both ends). Or expand prefix/suffix sums of length K.

questions.title: Sort Array by Frequency of Elements
questions.body: Glassdoor Java Developer interview: given array with duplicates, sort by occurrence count.
questions.answer:
Problem: Sort by frequency (higher first); ties by value (define order with interviewer).

Idea: count frequencies → sort unique keys with comparator (freq desc, value asc/desc) → expand back to array.

Complexity: O(N log U) for U unique keys. Alt: bucket sort by frequency for O(N + maxFreq) if values bounded.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Find First and Last Position in Sorted Array (Binary Search)
questions.body: SSE-2 Round 1, Nov 2023 (IIT candidate). Standard binary search for left boundary and right boundary.
questions.answer:
Problem: First and last index of target in a sorted array (with duplicates).

Idea — two binary searches:

  1. Lower bound: first index ≥ target (or == target).
  2. Upper bound: first index > target, then last = that − 1.

If lower bound misses target, return [-1,-1].

Complexity: O(log N). Do not scan linearly after finding one hit — that’s O(N) worst case on all duplicates.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Reverse Linked List in Groups of K
questions.body: Reverse Nodes in K-Group appeared in MMT Set-4 older rounds and in SSE-2 Round 1 (Nov 2023).
questions.answer:
Problem: Reverse nodes in groups of K; leftover < K stay as-is (usual LC #25 rule — confirm).

Idea:

  1. Count K nodes ahead; if fewer than K, stop.
  2. Reverse that segment in-place; connect previous group’s tail to new head; recurse/iterate on rest.

Complexity: O(N) time, O(1) extra (iterative) or O(N/K) recursion depth. Draw pointers on paper before coding.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: MMT Set-4 GFG, SSE-2 Nov 2023

questions.title: Clone Linked List with Next and Random Pointers
questions.body: F2F Round in MMT Set-4. Deep copy with both next and arbitrary pointers in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
questions.answer:
Problem: Deep-copy list where each node has next and random.

O(1) space weave method:

  1. Interleave copy nodes: A → A' → B → B'.
  2. Set A'.random = A.random.next (the copy sitting after original random).
  3. Unweave into original and clone lists.

Alt: HashMap old→new then second pass for random — O(N) space, simpler.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Populate Next Right Pointers in Each Node
questions.body: SDE-2 Round 1 (LeetCode Discuss 2025). Candidate was told O(log N) space solution also exists beyond O(N).
questions.answer:
Problem: Populate next pointers to the right sibling (perfect binary tree LC #116).

O(1) space: level by level using already-set next. For node with left/right: left.next = right; right.next = parent.next.left if parent.next exists.

Clarify: LC #117 (any tree) needs a different BFS/queue or carefully threaded approach. Comment space carefully — perfect-tree O(1) vs queue O(width).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists (Merge Point)
questions.body: F2F Round 3 (MMT Set-4 GFG).
questions.answer:
Problem: Find merge point of two singly linked lists (Y-shape).

Two-pointer switch: pointers traverse A then B (and vice versa). When lengths differ, after switch they align and meet at intersection (or both null).

Complexity: O(N+M) time, O(1) space. Alt: length diff method; HashSet of nodes.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Reverse Second Half of Linked List (In-Place)
questions.body: F2F Round 3 (MMT Set-4 GFG). In most efficient way (in-place).
questions.answer:
Problem: Reverse only the second half of the list in-place.

Steps:

  1. Guard empty / single node.
  2. Slow/fast to find mid (slow at end of first half).
  3. Standard iterative reverse from slow→next; reconnect slow→next = newHead.

Complexity: O(N) / O(1). Decide odd-length mid convention with interviewer (first half longer vs second).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: LCA / Common Manager of Two Employees
questions.body: Disguised as a real-world problem: "return the closest common manager of two employees". You can design the Emp class — the key insight is it's an LCA problem on a general tree, not necessarily a BST. MMT SDE/SSE-2 Round 1, Oct 2024. Also asked in campus rounds as standard binary tree LCA.
questions.answer:
Problem: LCA framed as “common manager” of two employees.

With parent pointers: walk both to root collecting ancestors; first shared is LCA. Or depth-align then climb together.

Classic BT LCA (no parent): recurse — if root is p or q return root; if both sides nonempty return root; else return nonempty side.

Complexity: O(N). Mention MMT often uses the org-chart / parent-pointer story.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SDE/SSE-2 LeetCode Oct 2024, Code360 Oct 2022
questions.hint: Disguised as "common manager" — it's LCA on a general tree. Key insight: if the Emp class has a parent pointer, walk both nodes to root, collect ancestors, find first match.

questions.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
questions.answer:
Problem: Validate BST — every node in (low, high) range.

Idea: DFS with bounds. Left child must be < node.val with updated high; right > node with updated low. Use long sentinels to avoid INT overflow.

Wrong approach: only check local parent-child — misses deeper violations.

Complexity: O(N). Inorder strictly increasing is an equivalent check.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Left View of Binary Tree
questions.body: Senior Software Engineer interview (GFG 2019). Recursive level-based approach.
questions.answer:
Problem: Left view — first node seen at each depth from the left.

DFS: preorder preferring left; record node when depth first visited.

BFS: level-order; take the first node of each level.

Complexity: O(N). Symmetric for right view (prefer right / take last in level).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Vertical Order Traversal of Binary Tree
questions.body: F2F Round 3 (MMT Set-4 GFG).
questions.answer:
Problem: Vertical order — group nodes by horizontal distance (root 0, left −1, right +1).

BFS + map: queue of (node, hd); insert into map<hd, list>. BFS keeps top-to-bottom order within a column. Sort keys for left→right output.

LC 987 also sorts by row then value — clarify which variant.

Complexity: O(N log C) if tree-map, C = distinct columns.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Path Finding in Binary Matrix (Backtracking / Rat in Maze)
questions.body: Technical Interview Round 1 (Software Engineer, 2020). Rat-in-a-maze style — find any path or longest path in binary matrix with walls.
questions.answer:
Problem: Path in binary matrix / rat-in-maze — move to destination on open cells.

Backtracking / DFS: mark visited, try 4 (or 8) directions, unmark on failure (if paths must reuse). BFS if only existence/shortest path needed.

Complexity: exponential worst-case for all paths; BFS shortest is O(N²) on grid.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Cut Tree to Minimise Subtree Sum Difference
questions.body: OA Round 2 (Software Engineer 2020). N nodes, N-1 edges. Each node has a value. Find edge to cut minimising |sum1 - sum2|.
questions.answer:
Problem: Remove one edge to minimise |sum(component1) − sum(component2)|.

Idea: total sum S. DFS returns subtree sum sub. Cutting the edge to parent splits into sub and S−sub; difference |S−2·sub|.

Critical: do not update the answer at the root (no edge above root) — that forces difference 0 incorrectly.

Complexity: O(N).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Critical Connections in Network (Bridges — Tarjan's)
questions.body: Naukri Code360 — SDE-1 campus (Sep/Oct 2022). Find all critical edges whose removal disconnects the network.
questions.answer:
Problem: Critical connections / bridges in an undirected graph.

Tarjan: discovery time tin, low-link low. Edge u–v is a bridge if low[v] > tin[u] (subtree of v can’t reach u or above).

Complexity: O(V+E). Handle multi-edges carefully; ignore parent edge in undirected DFS.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Shortest Path in Graph (Dijkstra)
questions.answer:
Problem: Shortest paths from a source on non-negative weighted graph.

Dijkstra: min-heap of (dist, node); relax neighbours when improvement found. Skip outdated heap entries.

Complexity: O((V+E) log V) binary heap. Not for negative weights — use Bellman-Ford. Unweighted → plain BFS.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Coordinate Reachability Check Using GCD
questions.body: OA Round 1 (Software Engineer 2020). Starting from (1,1), move to (a+b,b) or (a,a+b). Check if (x,y) is reachable. Hint: gcd(x,y) must equal 1.
questions.answer:
Problem: From (1,1) moves (a,b)→(a+b,b) or (a,a+b); can you reach (x,y)?

Insight: moves preserve gcd. Since gcd(1,1)=1, reachable iff gcd(x,y)==1 (for positive targets as stated).

Complexity: O(log min(x,y)). Confirm constraints (only positive quadrant, etc.).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: From (1,1) move to (a+b,b) or (a,a+b). Reach (x,y)? Key: gcd(x,y) must equal 1 since gcd is preserved by moves and gcd(1,1)=1.

questions.title: Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence
questions.body: SDE-2 (4 years exp) GFG — Round 1. Classic DP similar to LIS but maximising sum instead of length.
questions.answer:
Problem: Maximum sum of an increasing subsequence (not necessarily contiguous).

DP: dp[i] = val[i] + max{ dp[j] | j<i, val[j]<val[i] } (or just val[i]). Answer = max dp.

Complexity: O(N²). Mentions of O(N log N) usually refer to length (Patience LIS), not sum — different problem.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: dp[i] = max sum increasing subsequence ending at i. O(N²) naive, O(N log N) with BIT.

questions.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
questions.body: SDE-1 Backend (GFG 2022, 2024). Given an unsorted array, find the longest consecutive sequence. O(N) HashSet approach expected.
questions.answer:
Problem: Longest consecutive sequence in unsorted array — O(N) expected.

HashSet: insert all. Only start a streak at x when x−1 absent; count x, x+1, ….

Each number enters the inner loop once → O(N). Sorting would be O(N log N).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Put all nums in a HashSet. Only start a streak from x when x−1 is absent; walk x, x+1, … O(N).

questions.title: Generate All Permutations of a String
questions.body: SDE-1 Managerial round (GFG 2022 — selected). Recursive approach, recursion tree dry-run. Follow-up: handle duplicates using a Set.
questions.answer:
Problem: All permutations of a string / array.

Backtracking: swap-choose-recurse-unswap, or build path with used[]. Deduplicate with sort + skip identical siblings if duplicates exist.

Complexity: O(N·N!) time to output. Discuss heap’s algorithm only if asked.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Dice Throw — Count ways to achieve target sum
questions.body: Campus interview (Naukri Code360 Sep 2022). 2D DP problem.
questions.answer:
Problem: Number of ways to get sum X with N dice of F faces.

DP: dp[n][s] = ways with n dice summing to s. Transition: add face 1..F from dp[n−1][s−face].

Space-optimise to 1D rolling arrays. Mod 10^9+7 if required.

Complexity: O(N·X·F).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Generate N Pairs of Balanced Parentheses
questions.body: F2F Round 3 (MMT Set-4 GFG). Classic recursion/backtracking problem.
questions.answer:
Problem: All strings with N pairs of balanced parentheses.

Backtracking: place ( while open < N; place ) while close < open. Catalan number of results.

Complexity: O(C_n · n) output-sensitive. Classic recursion tree dry-run favourite.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Longest Repeating Non-Overlapping Substring
questions.body: Technical Round 2 (Software Engineer, 2020). Brute force → HashSet optimisation.
questions.answer:
Problem: Longest repeating non-overlapping substring (classic DP variant).

DP: dp[i][j] = length of repeating substring ending at i and j with no overlap (|i−j| > dp). Track global max length/substring.

Complexity: O(N²). Clarify exact GFG statement — definitions vary slightly.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Maximum Frequency Stack (FreqStack)
questions.body: SDE-1 Round 2 (GFG 2022, 2024). Design a stack that returns the most frequently pushed element. Complex data structure design using HashMap of stacks.
questions.answer:
Problem: FreqStack — push/pop; pop most frequent, ties → most recent.

Structure: val→freq map; freq→stack of vals; track maxfreq. Push updates freq and pushes into that freq’s stack. Pop from maxfreq stack; decrease freq; maybe decrement maxfreq.

Complexity: Amortised O(1) per op. Beautiful MMT/heap alternative discussion.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Kth Largest Element
questions.answer:
Problem: Kth largest in array (or stream).

Heap-of-K: min-heap size K; push if larger than top; top is Kth largest.

Complexity: O(N log K). Quickselect expected O(N). Stream variant: same heap maintained online.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SDE-2 Code360 May 2022, MMT Set-4

questions.title: LRU Cache
questions.body: Naukri Code360 SDE-1 Aug 2024 F2F (pen & paper round). Doubly linked list + HashMap. O(1) get and put.
questions.answer:
Problem: LRU Cache — O(1) get/put.

HashMap + doubly linked list: map key→node; list order = recency (head newest). get moves node to head; put updates/evicts tail when over capacity.

Complexity: O(1) average. Mention Java LinkedHashMap access-order as production shortcut, but implement DLL in interviews.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Stack Using Queue / Queue Using Stack
questions.body: Naukri Code360 SDE-1 campus Oct 2022.
questions.answer:
Problem: Implement stack using queues and/or queue using stacks.

Stack via queue: on push, enqueue then rotate older elements behind (or lazy on pop).

Queue via two stacks: in-stack for enqueue; out-stack for dequeue — pour when out empty (amortised O(1)).

State which variant you implement and complexity of each op.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Implement HashMap from Scratch — Thread-Safe
questions.category: Concurrency Coding (C++ reference; implement in Java at MMT)
questions.body: Senior Engineer Round 2 (GFG 2019) and Glassdoor Java Developer. Design put(), hashCode/equals, collision handling (chaining), then make put() thread-safe using synchronized. Follow-up: why default capacity is 16 (power of 2 for fast modulo via bitmask).
questions.answer:
Problem: Thread-safe HashMap from scratch (MMT loves Java follow-up).

Core: array of buckets; hash & (cap−1) requires power-of-two capacity; separate chaining; rehash at load factor 0.75.

Thread-safety: synchronize per bucket / striped locks (ConcurrentHashMap inspiration), or ConcurrentHashMap segments. Naive global synchronized is correct but contended.

Explain why capacity 16 and bitmask vs modulo — classic MMT Q.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: Senior SDE GFG 2019, Glassdoor Java Developer
questions.hint: MMT interviewers want you to implement this in Java with thread-safe put(). Follow-up: why default capacity is 16 (power-of-2 allows bitmask: hash & (n-1) instead of modulo).

questions.title: Multi-threaded HTML Word Counter
questions.category: Concurrency Coding (C++ reference; implement in Java at MMT)
questions.answer:
Problem: Download several HTML pages concurrently; count occurrences of a keyword; gather results.

Java approach: ExecutorService / CompletableFuture per URL; each task returns (url, keyword, count); AtomicInteger only if sharing one counter. Join with invokeAll / allOf.

Discuss timeouts, failure isolation, and not blocking the common ForkJoin pool on I/O — use a dedicated executor.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: Tech Lead LeetCode Discuss Jul 2024
questions.hint: Download pages concurrently, count string occurrences. Must use Java threading (CompletableFuture / ExecutorService). Output: [url, keyword, count].

questions.title: Thread-Safe Builder Pattern (AtomicReference approach)
questions.category: Concurrency Coding (C++ reference; implement in Java at MMT)
questions.answer:
Problem: Thread-safe Builder — interviewers may reject coarse synchronized.

Options:

  • Immutable builder: each setter returns a new builder copy — no shared mutable state.
  • AtomicReference<T>: CAS the product being built.

Explain why synchronized works but is “blocking”; show you know non-blocking alternatives.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: MMT interviewer rejected synchronized as "blocking". Expected Atomic-based or immutable builder solution.

questions.title: Tower of Hanoi
questions.body: On-campus technical round (SDE GFG). Classic recursion.
questions.answer:
Problem: Tower of Hanoi — move N disks from src to dest via aux.

Recurrence: move N−1 to aux, move largest to dest, move N−1 onto dest. T(N)=2T(N−1)+1 = 2^N−1 moves.

Dry-run N=3; mention stack depth O(N).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Classic recursion: move n−1 to aux, move largest to target, move n−1 onto target. T(n)=2T(n−1)+1.

questions.title: Shortest Unsorted Subarray
questions.answer:
Problem: Shortest unsorted continuous subarray that, if sorted, sorts the whole array.

Idea: find leftmost index not matching sorted order / or one-pass: track max from left and min from right to find the window boundaries.

Complexity: O(N) clever pass or O(N log N) via sorting copy. Edge: already sorted → length 0.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Josephus Problem — Circular array, remove Kth, find last
questions.body: CodingKaro SSE/SDE Round 1. Josephus Problem variant.
questions.answer:
Problem: Josephus — every K-th person eliminated in a circle; find survivor.

DP: f(1)=0 (0-based); f(n)=(f(n−1)+K) % n; convert to 1-based if needed.

Complexity: O(N). Simulation with queue is O(NK).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Prisoner Wall Jump Problem
questions.body: Online coding round (MMT Campus). N walls each with height h[i]. Max jump height = H. Rainy day — slips down l units after each jump. Count total jumps to escape.
questions.answer:
Problem: Prisoner jumps walls of heights h[i] with jump H and slip L each failed attempt.

Per wall: accumulate height += H each jump; if still below wall, slip −L and continue. Count jumps.

Critical: if H ≤ L, net progress after a failed jump is ≤0 → infinite loop on tall walls. Return −1 (impossible) unless h[i] ≤ H (cleared in one jump).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: For each wall, keep jumping +H and slipping −L until height clears the wall. If H ≤ L, only walls with height ≤ H are possible (one jump); taller walls are impossible.

questions.title: Store Open/Close Timing — Availability Check (Implementation)
questions.body: Tech Lead Coding Round 1 (LeetCode Discuss, Jul 2024). Given open and close time arrays of a store, implement availability check. Easy-level implementation question.

Idea: for each interval [open[i], close[i]) (clarify inclusive bounds), test membership. Or merge intervals then binary search.

Discuss midnight wrap-around if close < open (overnight hours).
